summary: The non_gaia project implements a crisis transport management system using Python with the CrewAI framework and six agents covering all major requirement areas. Every requirement has a corresponding agent role and at least one method stub, giving good structural coverage. However, the implementation has a critical operational bug — tasks created in run_simulation are never passed to the Crew, so Crew.kickoff() executes with an empty task list — and all agents have empty tools lists, meaning they cannot perform any real actions. Timestamps are hardcoded strings across all agents, and there is no inter-agent communication mechanism beyond CrewAI's LLM-mediated task delegation.

findings.description: The Crew is initialised with tasks=[] in setup_crew(), then a list of Task objects is created in run_simulation() but is never assigned to self.crew. Crew.kickoff() executes with an empty task list, making the entire simulation a no-op.
findings.evidence: main.py line 32: 'self.crew = Crew(agents=..., tasks=[], ...)'. Lines 43–73: tasks list created locally. Line 77: 'result = self.crew.kickoff()' — crew.tasks is still [].

findings.description: All six agents have empty tools lists (tools=[]). CrewAI agents without tools rely solely on LLM text generation and cannot call any external system, query databases, or take real actions. The system cannot function beyond producing text output.
findings.evidence: resource_requester.py line 11: 'self.tools = []'. Same pattern in resource_provider.py, route_planner.py, traffic_monitor.py, notification.py, emergency_response.py.

findings.description: No resource matching logic is implemented. ResourceProviderAgent.find_available_resources checks a hardcoded lookup dict and returns availability status, but there is no mechanism that connects a requester's need to a provider's supply and confirms a match.
findings.evidence: resource_provider.py lines 25–51: find_available_resources uses a static dict {'medical_supplies': [...], 'fuel': [...], 'equipment': [...]}. No matching agent or method links this to ResourceRequesterAgent.

findings.description: All timestamps in all agent files are hardcoded to the literal string '2023-05-15 14:30:00'. Every notification, route update, and incident report will carry this static timestamp regardless of when events actually occur.
findings.evidence: notification.py line 29: '"timestamp": "2023-05-15 14:30:00"'. Same pattern in route_planner.py line 37, traffic_monitor.py line 48, emergency_response.py lines 33 and 45.

findings.description: Incident IDs are generated using hash(location) % 10000, producing values in [0, 9999]. Different locations can produce the same incident ID, making records non-unique and potentially overwriting each other.
findings.evidence: traffic_monitor.py line 43: '"incident_id": f"incident_{hash(location) % 10000}"'. emergency_response.py line 28: same pattern.

findings.description: print() statements are used as the notification mechanism throughout all agent files. These are debug artifacts with no actual delivery infrastructure.
findings.evidence: notification.py line 35: 'print(f"Notification sent to {recipient}: {message}")'. route_planner.py line 39: 'print(f"Route Planned: {start_location} to {end_location}")'. Same pattern in all agents.

findings.description: The agent helper methods (process_request, find_available_resources, plan_route, etc.) are defined on the Python wrapper classes but are not exposed as CrewAI tools. They are unreachable through the crew execution model and exist only as dead code relative to the framework.
findings.evidence: resource_requester.py lines 25–43: process_request and get_request_status defined on ResourceRequesterAgent, but create_agent() returns a crewai.Agent that has no reference to these methods.

findings.description: Route updating on accidents depends entirely on LLM reasoning within the CrewAI task, with no structured data model or update protocol. The RoutePlannerAgent.update_route method exists but returns a dict with a hardcoded updated_time string and is not connected to the crew.
findings.evidence: route_planner.py lines 64–73: update_route returns {'route_id': route_id, 'updated_time': '2023-05-15 14:30:00', ...}. Not registered as a crew tool.

findings.description: All six requirement areas (resource requesting, resource providing, route planning, traffic monitoring, general notifications, and emergency service notifications) have dedicated agent roles, providing good structural requirement coverage.
findings.evidence: main.py lines 22–28: six agents initialised — resource_requester, resource_provider, route_planner, traffic_monitor, notification, emergency_response.

findings.description: RoutePlannerAgent explicitly implements both find_alternative_routes (returns multiple alternatives with reason strings) and update_route, directly reflecting two distinct requirements.
findings.evidence: route_planner.py lines 43–73: find_alternative_routes returns a list of two alternative route dicts with distance, estimated_time, and reason fields.

missing_requirements: Dopasowywanie dostępnych zasobów do potrzeb — no matching logic connects requester needs to provider availability; find_available_resources checks a hardcoded dict but never links to an actual request
Aktualizacja obecnej trasy w razie wypadków losowych — update_route exists as a stub but is not wired into the crew execution and uses a hardcoded timestamp
logical_inconsistencies: Crew is created with tasks=[] and kickoff() is called without any tasks being assigned, making the simulation produce no output beyond the framework startup
Agent helper methods are defined on Python wrapper classes but never registered as CrewAI tools, making them unreachable during crew execution
Resource matching depends on two agents (requester and provider) coordinating, but there is no shared state or message protocol between them — only LLM-mediated task text
implementation_risks: Crew.kickoff() with empty tasks list: the simulation silently completes with no work done and no error raised
Hardcoded timestamps on all records make audit trails and time-based ordering impossible in production
Hash-based IDs guarantee collisions at scale; in a crisis scenario with many simultaneous incidents, records could silently overwrite each other
